## Why four frequencies sound like one note

Play a sine wave at 220 Hz, then add sines at 440, 660 and 880 Hz. How many
notes should you hear? You get one, with a different colour. All four start together and
share a whole-number relationship, and your ear gathers them into a single
pitched sound instead of a chord.

Each component is a *partial*. When the partial frequencies land at `1f`, `2f`,
`3f`, `4f` and so on, they belong to the *harmonic series* above a fundamental
frequency `f`, and their relative amplitudes are most of what you hear as
colour. This program stores that colour as a short profile of `[multiple, level]`
pairs and builds it up one component at a time.

Listen to the bare 220 Hz sine first, and hold that thin reference in your head
as the upper components arrive. The pitch should stay anchored around A3 while
brightness and edge accumulate on top of it.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60

base_hz = 220.0
partials = [[1, 0.8], [2, 0.35], [3, 0.2], [4, 0.12]]

define :additive_tone do |base, profile|
  profile.each do |multiple, level|
    synth :sine, note: hz_to_midi(base * multiple), amp: level,
      attack: 0.05, sustain: 1.5, release: 0.4
  end
  sleep 2.2
end

1.upto(partials.length) do |count|
  additive_tone base_hz, partials.take(count)
  sleep 0.5
end
```

Pass one is the fundamental alone, and it sounds plain, almost characterless.
Each pass after that keeps everything you've already heard and adds one higher
partial, so what arrives is a brighter, firmer edge, not a new pitch. Watch out
for one confound: the last pass is also louder in total. Keep the level moderate
so you can tell added energy apart from added colour.

## Three profiles worth hearing

1. Set every amplitude to `0.25`. The fundamental loses its dominance and the
   upper partials push forward, giving you a harder, thinner compound tone. Some
   of what you hear is the change in total loudness, so allow for that.

2. Restore the profile, then delete the second partial and keep the third and
   fourth. The fundamental still tells you the pitch, but the missing octave
   leaves a hole in the balance above it. Compare directly against the original;
   describing the gap from memory won't work.

3. Restore everything and change the base from 220 to 165 Hz. Every component
   moves, since all of them derive from that base. The harmonic relationships
   survive intact, though your speakers and your own hearing will make the
   balance feel different down there.

Restore the reference between each edit. One audible cause at a time is the
entire point.

## Why the components fuse

Additive synthesis builds a complex waveform by summing simple ones. In this
profile, the frequency multipliers choose the components and the amplitudes
weight them. The fundamental supplies the main repetition rate and a strong
pitch cue. The upper components reshape the waveform *within* each cycle, which
is how you change timbre without touching the fundamental.

They fuse partly because their cycles keep aligning. At 220 Hz, the fundamental
finishes one cycle while 440 finishes two, 660 finishes three and 880 finishes
four. At the end of the fundamental's cycle, all four arrive back at a shared
boundary together. That short repeating compound pattern is what supports the
impression of one note.

This four-sine sound is a model, not a real instrument. Acoustic tones usually
begin with noise, shift their spectral balance while they sound, and contain
components that sit slightly off exact integer multiples. The small model earns
its place by exposing one mechanism where a preset synth would bury it.

Amplitude needs watching whenever you're adding signals. Four components at
`0.8` can produce a combined peak far larger than any single synth call
suggests. The falling levels in the original profile give you headroom and also
resemble the declining upper spectrum of many real sounds. If an edited profile
distorts, drop all the levels before concluding anything about timbre.
Distortion generates its own upper frequencies, and loudness will happily
impersonate brightness.

Notice how much you can learn before playback. You can inspect the multiples,
compare two amplitude curves, or calculate the highest frequency without
rendering a note. Sound then gives those numbers perceptual meaning. [Lesson 5](05-consonance-small-whole-numbers.qmd)
takes the same alignment idea further: when two fundamentals sit in a small
whole-number ratio, some of the partials above them coincide.

## Take it further

Build two four-partial profiles over the same 220 Hz fundamental. Give the first
a steep amplitude decline. In the second, strengthen the third and fourth
partials while keeping enough headroom to stay clean. Alternate them four times
without changing the base frequency or the envelope.

Print both profiles and find the partial whose amplitude differs most. Then
listen to the alternation in Sonic Pi 5 at a moderate level, and describe the
change using a feature you can point at: a harder edge, a more hollow middle,
more brightness. The unchanged pitch is part of the result. You've succeeded when
the colour moves and A3 stays exactly where it was.
